description_top: Counting clicks sounds like n = n + 1. At thirty million events a second, with retries, phones that were offline for a day and a fraud team that changes its mind a week later, the hard part is counting once, in the right hour, and proving it. A Staff-bar (L6/L7) reference solution run like a real round: the design starts as a C4 container view and evolves only because an interviewer breaks it, six times, with each mechanism and technology introduced at the moment it is needed. {DURATION} minutes, {SLIDES} numbered slides.

The thesis: count once, from one log, with one piece of code run twice, fast and provisional for the dashboard, exact and pinned for the bill. Never increment a number you can recompute: replace it, and keep every version you billed.

IN THIS VIDEO
• Estimates from one scale line: 10 M events a second, 6 GB/s at peak, 0.7 TB of dedup state, and $375 M a month in duplicate clicks if retries are not removed
• V1 → V2 → V3 on one C4 container view, with component zooms for every fix
• Six challenges: a dashboard that must be 10 s fresh, the same click three times (and a four-hour replay), late and skewed events, one ad at 2 million a second, fraud after the invoice, and a wrong number nobody notices
• Mechanisms where they are needed: one aggregation run twice, event IDs, watermarks, two-stage aggregation, replace-not-increment, versions and adjustments

HOW TO USE IT
Run the round cold first. Then watch once straight through. On the second pass, pause after each interviewer question and answer it first.

The technical content has not been reviewed by a person.

post: "Use exactly-once" is the answer that fails the ad-click question. The grade is on what you do instead.

I've published a {DURATION}-minute reference solution for counting ad impressions and clicks at the Staff bar, run like a real round: one C4 diagram that evolves through six interviewer challenges, on {SLIDES} numbered slides.

The idea that unlocks it: one log, one aggregation code run twice. Fast and provisional for the dashboard, exact and pinned for the bill, and every number replaced by key rather than incremented, so a retry, a replay or a fraud correction can never double anything.

What it goes into:
→ The same click three times, and why the broker's exactly-once doesn't help
→ Yesterday's events at 6 a.m., and a clock that says 2031
→ One ad at 2 million impressions a second
→ Fraud after the invoice, without editing it
Best on a second pass: pause after each question and answer it first.
It's a scripted walkthrough with synthetic voices, built with Claude Code from design-room, my open-source system design interview simulator.
Where does your pipeline decide which hour an event belongs to?
